lesson.title: Turning a List Around: The reverse() Method
lesson.summary: The reverse() method flips the order of a list's elements in place, permanently changing the original list instead of building a new one.
lesson.body:
You already know that lists come with built in methods like append() and sort() that change a list without you having to write a loop yourself. The reverse() method belongs to that same family. Call it on any list and Python walks through the list and rearranges the elements so the last one becomes first and the first becomes last, all without creating a second list in memory.

The detail that trips up almost every new programmer is that reverse() returns None. It is a method that mutates the list and hands back nothing useful, exactly like append() and sort(). If you write new_list = old_list.reverse(), expecting new_list to hold the reversed data, you will instead store None and lose track of the reversed list entirely, because the real result was already written into old_list itself.

Here is reverse() used correctly:

```python
scores = [55, 92, 78, 61, 88]
scores.reverse()
print(scores)
```

This prints:

```
[88, 61, 78, 92, 55]
```

Now compare that to the mistake described above:

```python
scores = [55, 92, 78, 61, 88]
backwards = scores.reverse()
print(backwards)
print(scores)
```

This prints:

```
None
[88, 61, 78, 92, 55]
```

Notice that scores did get reversed since the method still mutated it, but backwards is useless because reverse() never returns the list itself. If you need a reversed copy while keeping the original list untouched, use slicing instead, such as scores[::-1], which builds a brand new list and leaves scores exactly as it was. The rule to remember is that a method changes the object it is called on, and you only need to capture a return value when the method actually produces one.
